newsitem.title: USA: Local labor tight, wage pressures seen -- Dallas Fed.
newsitem.headline: Local labor tight, wage pressures seen -- Dallas Fed.

text.p: Labor markets are very tight across the board in the 11th U.S. economic district, with some scattered wage pressures seen in specific areas, a Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas economist said.
"As a whole, labor markets are tight ... with the exception of near the (Mexican) borders," D'Ann Petersen, economist at the Dallas Fed, told Reuters.
"A lot of companies are reporting that they're having a hard time finding all types of workers, including low-skilled workers as well as high-skilled workers," she added.
Petersen said the firmness in the local labor markets has sparked some wage pressures. But she added the pressures were mostly concentrated in specific sectors.
"There have been scattered reports of people having to raise salaries in order to attract workers, but there is no real widespread evidence yet. We're still hearing scattered reports," Petersen said.
The Dallas Fed serves the nation's 11th economic district, which includes the state of Texas, northern Louisiana and southern New Mexico.

Petersen said the region's employment growth rate is currently close to 2.0 percent, which she considered to be moderate. The Dallas Fed economist said job growth was expected to hold steady through 1997.

"(The economy) has slowed from the rapid rates of growth earlier in the nineties, but it's still moving along quite comfortably. It's growing close to a 2.0 percent rate of employment growth," Petersen said.
The Dallas Fed economist also said ratail sales were strong, suggesting consumers were confident about the economy.
"Retail sales were not so good last year, but they're starting to pick up again," she said, adding that retailers have reported sales are growing at a "healthy rate."
Peterson also pointed to a strong oil industry as a reason behind the region's current economic vigor.
"We've seen a lot of drilling activity. In Houston, they're talking about not being able to find enough people for the rigs," she said.
"So the oil industry is doing quite well even though it's much smaller now than it used to be in the eighties," Petersen added.

Construction was seen as contributing to the local economy's health as well. Growth in high-technology industries, mainly in the Austin region, was also pointed to as a factor keeping the economy alive.

The Dallas Fed is headed by Robert McTeer, a member of the central bank's policy setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). McTeer is not scheduled to vote on FOMC policy action in 1997 given the committee's rotation rules.
The Federal Reserve last changed short-term rates on March 25, when the central bank raised its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent.
